doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Life lessons, Hugh Masekela and the African rhythms behind jazz
summary: He says to put the music first, tells how Masekela corrected his cha-cha as a Mozambican rhythm, and traces how African music evolved differently across the Americas.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What kind of life lessons did you learn along the way from Ray Charles or Rahsaan or Dizzy? Something beyond the music?

Well it’s all connected. It’s all connected. If you’ve going to really play this music you’ve got to live the music. And you always put the music first. People that are entertainers — well a musician is an entertainer of sorts — but there’s a deeper quality to it as well. It’s not just the comedian or an actor or a fashion show. It’s a sound. And you’re there to make a sound. That sound should be the focus of your presentation and it’s what you’re sharing, whatever it is that you can make the sound do, you’re sharing that with your audience you see? I’m going to tell you a story. I used to work with Hugh Masekela. And you know we were playing this song and it was a very similar rhythm to the cha-cha. And you know he was from South Africa. And so I had some clave, because I play Latin music a lot. I started playing the clave and he looked at me smiling, and I didn’t know any better, so I say, “cha-cha.” And he looked at me and said, “No, that ain’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

no cha-cha” and he named some African name that I couldn’t pronounce to you now, I don’t remember. He said blah-blah-blah. That’s a rhythm from Mozambique. I said, “Yes, sir, okay.” Because that’s where it comes from, you see? That’s where it comes from. So you know all this music, all the African people that were brought here against their will not only came to North America, they went to the Caribbean, to South America, and depending on who their colonizers were the music evolved differently. In Portugal you have the samba, bossa nova; in the Caribbean you have Afro-Cuban and soca and calypso and merengue and cumbia, plena, and bomba and so many forms. And then in America we have the blues which evolved into jazz. Blues is the root. And in America it evolved differently because the English were scared of the rhythm. They took the drum away. In Latin America they didn’t take the drum away. On Sunday, when the other people went to church they were allowed to play the drum to keep some semblance of the culture. So the music evolved differently because of that. And in America it evolved a unique way because you know if you know anything about traditional African drum ensemble, they had the iron bells and they had the higher pitched drum, the djembe, and then they have lower pitched drums, the dundun, and some even have bigger bass drums. And all those different elements were put into a drumset. The cymbal became the bell, the tom-tom and snare is a djembe, the high voice. And so one person is doing what was many people. And you know it evolved differently because of that. Can you imagine if black people were allowed to have copyrights the man who invented the drumset, they’d be a billionaire by now.
So all those kind of things are relevant to the music. The music is an expression of all of that.
